Great piece on Osmo a company by Alex Wiltschko @awiltschko that wants to democratize scent, or as Lux Capital's Josh Wolfe @wolfejosh says, "Shazam for smell." A quick watch, otherwise some takeaways:

* Osmo's pitch is "perfume now, disease detection down the line." The frame is that sight became pixels and sound became waveforms, and smell was the last sense no machine could read or reproduce. Osmo says it has closed that gap and can turn a single text or image prompt into a finished scent in 48 hours, reversing how scent is designed and delivered.

* The mission is taking on the gatekeepers, which Alex calls "democratizing scent." Fortune frames Osmo as building the world's first "olfactory intelligence," an AI trained to predict what a molecule smells like before anyone synthesizes it. The predict-first claim is the whole company. If a model can name a smell from a structure, the trial-and-error bench chemistry that kept scent slow and secretive becomes searchable.

* The target is the supplier layer of a $30 billion market four giants have run. Four giant suppliers have dominated the flavor and fragrance business for decades, and that the brands consumers recognize don't formulate their own scent, they buy it. Osmo isn't chasing the bottle, it wants to be the platform the bottle's maker buys from. The incumbents' weakness is speed and scale: they often take months and many require bulk orders, which leaves smaller brands underserved. A predict-and-produce pipeline that fills a small order fast is aimed straight at that gap.

* Josh Wolfe's consumer picture is a "Shazam for smell." Walk into a room, press a button, and identify the perfume or cologne the way Shazam names a song. Identifying a scent and generating one are two directions of the same map between molecules and perception. The read direction is the demo that makes the idea land in a room. The write direction, generating a scent to order, is where Osmo's revenue actually sits.

* Josh Wolfe's test for deep-science hype is three words, "does it work." Lux Capital was an early Osmo backer and helped raise $60 million for its 2023 launch. Wolfe's filter for a hard-science pitch: past the PhD-level sophistication, it comes down to whether it works, framed as a poker game of "how much capital accomplishes what, but in what period of time and who will care."

* The technical unlock was borrowed from drug-discovery AI: graph neural networks. The methods that cracked images and language assume a regular shape, a grid of pixels or a line of text. Molecules don't have one. As Wiltschko puts it, they are "atoms that click together in all kinds of different shapes," so Osmo used graph neural networks, a technique developed to handle exactly that kind of irregular input, the same family of AI built to discover new drugs. The bet is that a representation that predicts whether a molecule binds a protein can predict whether it smells like a plum.

* Osmo says in 2024 it encoded or "teleported" a real plum's smell as data and rebuilt it across the lab with no human involved. The productized version, Osmo Studio, takes text or image and converts it into scent, which is how the film generated the smell of the New York Stock Exchange, iterating from "woody floral earthy" to a match. Wiltschko puts the tool in familiar company: it's "like using Canva or Photoshop or Figma," with the human as the designer.

* The business runs two revenue lines off one asset, and AW keeps it B2B on purpose. Osmo spent about 2.5 years in pure R&D because the science was the risk. After it "teleported a scent," the fastest-growing parts became manufacturing and sales. It sells finished fragrance to fast-growing emerging brands and sells software and data access to the large companies that already trade in smell. Wiltschko's reason for avoiding B2C is discipline: a consumer brand can win on story and coast, while a supplier has to keep beating century-old incumbents on the science, which forces the research to keep moving.

* The moat is data and a patent lead. Where a chemist tests one molecule at a time, Osmo says it screens billions at once and keeps only the best. On top of that sit four company assertions: 10x higher success rates, 5x lower cost than industry norms, more new fragrance-ingredient patents than the rest of the industry combined in 2025, and up to 250 molecules per patent against the traditional one or two.

* For a company selling automation, Osmo insists on the humans, led by master perfumer Christophe Laudamiel. Fortune's framing is that AI expedites molecule discovery while humans remain the artists. The lab tour makes it literal: robots run samples day and night to feed the model the data it needs, and every robot has a name, one is Taylor Swift. Laudamiel, whom the film calls one of the few master perfumers in the world, describes his job as learning to "get into AI and now to steer it as well." To customers the model is a design tool, to the craft it's an instrument a perfumer plays.

* The endgame is disease detection, and for Alex it's personal. Fragrance, in Osmo's telling, is the commercial work that funds the harder science. The premise: dogs, with far sharper noses, have been trained to detect COVID, cancer, Parkinson's, and Alzheimer's, each of which leaves a scent signature. If a machine could read those signatures, screening would get close to free. Wiltschko is explicit that making fragrances generates the data that strengthens the platform, so the two lines are one flywheel. Then he makes it personal: his father died of brain cancer, a condition some evidence suggests carries a unique scent, and uncovering those molecules is the mission underneath the company.

Not Everything is For Everyone, and that's a Good Thing

The AI good, AI bad debate.
The "people don't read books anymore" panic.
The "Education isn't teaching practical skills" outrage.

The ongoing discontent in these tangential spaces boil down to one core sentiment:

"This good thing, that undeniably is good for society, should be instilled in everyone."

And, consequently,

"Because not everyone possesses, appreciates, or actively partakes this undeniably good thing for society, our civilization is in crisis."

We see this in the explosion of comments too frequently echoed: 
"AI is essential for those who couldn't to finally create art!"
"A post-literacy culture will create a dangerous bifurcation of literati vs the illiterate!"
"Education is not preparing the next generation for jobs and survival!"

I particularly do not understand it when it is the anti-communist, freedom-loving, personal-responsibility touting conservatives that clutch their pearls and gasp in such like fashion.

We have gone from "Of course everyone needs to go to college," realizing that that path doesn't work, promoting alternatives like entrepreneurship and trade skills, to now coming full circle again ---

"Of course everyone should A, B, C!"

Because the thought, once more, since no lesson has been learned, is that an elevated civilization means everyone is intelligent, productive, resourceful, driven ... in THIS particular way, or else DOOM.

I propose that an elevated civilization truly only  needs these basic elements:

1.Accountability Culture.
2.Desire to Strive for Personal Betterment.
3. Looking Up to Godliness.

Foster these, and the rest will take care of itself, in whatever form it will look like, in however it needs to look like.

That extra lift of limit on Grok Imagine?
The beautiful library of physical books?
That state-funded mandatory Home economics class?

Bells and Whistles.

The truth is, America is over-abundant -- everything can be obtained, to a degree of manner, for free, for cheap, and nigh on instantly.

The ones that are creating art, that are sitting brooding over dense great books, the ones that are solving problems... They've been doing it long before it was convenient.

The ones who haven't done so, will not even with a magic spoon.

And those in between? They are doing their thing, in ways unconventional and unfamiliar. 

We need to rein back on the obsession over Democratizing everything under the sun. Not everything is for everyone, and that is a good thing.

Thrilled to see the @AppliedSciAI literature agent win the Best AI Scientist award at one of the world's leading ML conferences 🤯

You can try the agent in the link below.

Some of its killer features come from the insight that the signals that often matter most in a scientific paper aren't in the text - they're scattered across figures, tables, gels, micrographs and electrophysiology traces.

It was inspiring to watch @lukasweidener @markoasi1 & @mihailoxyz attack this problem and build an agent that hit SOTA across major literature search benchmarks like LitQA3, FigQA2 & TableQA2. 

ASI is focused on cardiac risk, using model-assay loops to build a “virtual heart” that predicts cardiac safety for small molecules, guides lead optimization and could eventually power digital twins in clinical trials. Our team runs the agent for internal R&D and to generate training data for our cardiac safety models.

Concrete case: when CardioSafe flags a compound as toxic and its RL mode proposes safer analogs, the literature agent checks whether anyone has already assayed a close neighbor - so we’re not spending months on a "safer" molecule someone else quietly killed years ago.

That answer almost never lives in the text of a paper, rather it’s usually in a dose-response curve, summplementary assay table or ion-channel panel buried in a figure. It's a good example of how prediction models paired with scientific reasoning creates new capabilities in drug discovery.

Try ASI’s literature agent + CardioSafe today: https://t.co/r7HFewNhIA

The model humans prefer the most is not always the most accurate one!

Arena just added factuality scoring to their leaderboard alongside human preference. The idea: human preference measures whether a response felt good to read. Factuality measures the correctness of claims in a model's response. These are two different things.

Most benchmarks test models on fixed, predetermined questions in a lab setting. What Arena is doing differently: measuring factuality in real, open-ended user conversations at scale.

Over 2 million claims extracted from actual conversations, verified against the web, across 130k Text Arena battles and 40k Search Arena battles.

The way it works: they randomly sample battles, extract web-verifiable claims from each model response, verify them against the web, and calculate a factuality score per model. The final ranking is a weighted combination of human preference and factuality score.

When factuality weight is enabled, the shifts are significant. In Text Arena, GPT-5.5 jumps 13 spots. Muse Spark drops 13. Claude Fable 5 moves down slightly. In Search Arena, GPT-5.5-search takes the top spot while Gemini grounding drops from 7 to 13.

I've shared the full methodology blog in the replies!
